questions.question: How do you configure Azure Application Insights for observability in a Spring Boot application?
questions.title: Azure Application Insights for Spring Boot Observability
questions.direct_answer: Add the Application Insights Java agent (applicationinsights-agent.jar) as a JVM argument. It auto-instruments Spring Boot, captures distributed traces, exceptions, and custom metrics without code changes, forwarding everything to Azure Monitor.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of APM instrumentation in Java — specifically the agent-based auto-instrumentation approach vs. manual SDK calls.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Embedding the Application Insights SDK into application code with manual track*() calls instead of using the zero-code Java agent.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention distributed tracing via W3C TraceContext propagation, Log4j/SLF4J correlation ID injection, and Live Metrics for real-time monitoring.

sections.title: When a Request Takes 12 Seconds, You Need to Know Where the Time Went
sections.content:
When a user reports that an API call took 12 seconds, you need to know where that time was spent — was it the database query, the downstream HTTP call, or the garbage collector? Without an APM tool, the answer requires correlating timestamps across application logs, database slow query logs, and infrastructure metrics. Azure Application Insights solves this with distributed tracing that stitches every operation — HTTP request, JDBC query, outbound HTTP call, message processing — into a single trace.

The critical decision for Java developers is *how* to instrument. The old approach was embedding the Application Insights SDK into your code with manual `telemetryClient.trackEvent()` and `trackDependency()` calls scattered across services. The modern approach is the **Java agent** (`applicationinsights-agent.jar`), which uses bytecode instrumentation to auto-instrument the entire Spring Boot stack without touching your source code. The agent hooks into JDBC drivers, HTTP client libraries, Spring MVC, messaging frameworks, and more — all through a single JVM argument.

The agent is built on OpenTelemetry internally, which means it propagates the W3C `traceparent` header across services. When Service A calls Service B, both operations appear in the same distributed trace in the Azure portal. It also injects the trace ID into SLF4J's MDC, so every log line includes the trace and span ID — making log-to-trace correlation trivial.

sections.title: One JVM Argument, Zero Code Changes, Full Stack Coverage
sections.content:
The setup requires downloading the agent JAR and adding a JVM argument. No Maven dependencies, no code changes to your application.

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY applicationinsights-agent.jar .
COPY target/app.jar .
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-javaagent:applicationinsights-agent.jar", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

The agent reads its configuration from `applicationinsights.json` in the same directory or classpath root.

```json
{
  "connectionString": "InstrumentationKey=...",
  "role": { "name": "order-api" },
  "sampling": { "percentage": 10 }
}
```

The `role.name` identifies this service in multi-service traces — the Application Map in the Azure portal uses this name to draw the service dependency graph. The `connectionString` comes from the Application Insights resource. Sampling percentage controls what fraction of telemetry is collected.

For custom business metrics, use **Micrometer** — Spring Boot's default metrics facade. The agent exports Micrometer metrics automatically through its bridge, so `Counter`, `Timer`, and `Gauge` beans flow into Azure Monitor without additional configuration or exporter setup.

sections.title: Distributed Traces and Log Correlation — One ID Across Every Service
sections.content:
The agent propagates W3C `traceparent` headers on all outbound HTTP calls. When `order-api` calls `inventory-api`, both services' spans share the same trace ID and appear in a single end-to-end transaction view in the Azure portal.

Log correlation is equally powerful. The agent injects `trace_id` and `span_id` into SLF4J's MDC context. If your log pattern includes `%X{trace_id}`, every log line is tagged with the distributed trace ID.

```xml
<pattern>%d{HH:mm:ss} [%thread] [trace=%X{trace_id} span=%X{span_id}] %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n</pattern>
```

This means you can take a trace ID from the Azure portal's transaction view, search for it in Log Analytics, and find every log line from every service that participated in that request. During incident investigation, this eliminates the 'which service logged what?' question entirely.

Application Insights also captures unhandled exceptions with the full stack trace, dependency durations, and request/response metadata. The **Application Map** visualizes service dependencies with health indicators — if `order-api` calls `payment-api` and payment-api's average response time degrades, the map highlights that edge in red. This gives on-call engineers a 30-second overview of system health that would otherwise require checking multiple dashboards.

sections.title: 100% Sampling at High Traffic Can Cost Hundreds Per Month
sections.content:
**Uncontrolled telemetry ingestion is the most expensive mistake** with Application Insights. At 100% sampling and 10,000 requests per second, a single service can generate over $500/month in ingestion costs. The agent's default adaptive sampling dynamically reduces volume during traffic spikes while preserving full traces for errors, slow requests, and dependency failures.

Set a **daily cap** in the Azure portal as a safety net — once the cap is reached, Application Insights stops ingesting new telemetry but continues processing alerts on existing data. Configure fixed sampling at 10% for high-traffic services (capturing every 10th request end-to-end) and leave error traces at 100% — failed requests should always be fully captured.

For actionable alerting, define rules based on SLO thresholds rather than absolute values. Alert when p99 latency exceeds 2 seconds for 5 consecutive minutes, or when error rate exceeds 1% over a 10-minute window. Azure Monitor's **smart detection** adapts to your traffic patterns and flags anomalies without manual threshold configuration — but it supplements, not replaces, explicit SLO-based alerts.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Java agent instruments without code changes** — `-javaagent:applicationinsights-agent.jar` auto-collects HTTP metrics, SQL queries, outbound calls, and exceptions; no SDK imports in business code
- **`APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING` is the only required config** — contains instrumentation key and regional endpoint; set as environment variable; agent picks it up automatically
- **Distributed trace correlation across services** — agent propagates trace IDs through HTTP headers; a slow request can be traced from API gateway through each microservice to the database query
- **Micrometer metrics auto-collected by the agent** — custom `Counter`, `Timer`, and `Gauge` metrics appear in Application Insights as custom metrics without any Insights SDK calls
- **KQL for querying telemetry** — `requests | where success == false | summarize count() by bin(timestamp, 1h)` queries error rates by hour; create alerts directly from KQL results in the portal

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Application Insights provides distributed tracing, metrics, and log aggregation for Spring Boot services on Azure — the recommended approach is the Java agent, not the SDK, because the agent instruments the application without any code changes.

**Java agent — zero-code instrumentation**
- Attach the agent as a JVM argument: `-javaagent:/path/to/applicationinsights-agent.jar`; in App Service, set `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-javaagent:/path/applicationinsights-agent.jar` in the application settings
- The agent auto-instruments HTTP requests (request duration, status codes), Spring Data queries (SQL timing, query text), outbound HTTP calls, and exception logging — all without any application code changes
- Application Insights collects this telemetry and correlates it with a distributed trace ID, which means a slow API call can be traced through the Spring Boot service to the database query that caused it

**Connection string configuration**
- Configure `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING` as an environment variable or application setting — this is the only configuration the agent needs; the connection string includes the instrumentation key and the regional endpoint

**Custom telemetry with Micrometer**
- The Application Insights Java agent integrates with Micrometer automatically — custom `Counter`, `Timer`, and `Gauge` metrics registered with the `MeterRegistry` are published to Application Insights as custom metrics
- Use `TelemetryClient` from the Application Insights SDK for custom events and properties: `telemetryClient.trackEvent("OrderPlaced", properties, metrics)` adds domain events to the telemetry stream

**Querying with Kusto (KQL)**
- Application Insights stores telemetry in Log Analytics; queries use Kusto Query Language: `requests | where duration > 500 | summarize count() by bin(timestamp, 5m)` finds slow requests per 5-minute window
- Create dashboards and alerts directly in Application Insights from KQL queries

questions.question: How does Azure API Management work with Spring Boot microservices?
questions.title: Azure API Management for Spring Boot Microservices
questions.direct_answer: Azure API Management acts as a gateway in front of your Spring Boot services, providing rate limiting, authentication, request transformation, caching, and developer portal — without modifying your backend code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of API gateway patterns and what APIM adds over deploying Spring Boot services directly — especially policy-based cross-cutting concerns.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reimplementing rate limiting, authentication, and request validation inside each Spring Boot service instead of centralizing them in APIM policies.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention APIM policy expressions (C#-like), the self-hosted gateway for hybrid deployments, and OpenAPI spec import for automatic API definition.

sections.title: Why Twenty Services Shouldn't Each Build Their Own Rate Limiter
sections.content:
Every Spring Boot microservice needs rate limiting, authentication, request validation, and logging. The naive approach is implementing these as filters or interceptors in each service — which means every team builds their own rate limiter, every service parses JWTs independently, and cross-cutting policy changes require redeploying every service. Azure API Management centralizes these concerns in a gateway layer that sits in front of your services.

APIM's key insight is the **policy pipeline**. Instead of writing Java code for gateway concerns, you configure XML-based policies that execute in four stages: inbound (before the request reaches your service), backend (the request forwarding), outbound (before the response returns to the client), and on-error (exception handling). Rate limiting, JWT validation, request transformation, response caching, and CORS headers are all configurable policies — no backend code changes required.

The mistake most candidates make is reimplementing these cross-cutting concerns inside each Spring Boot service. A rate limiter built with Bucket4j works for one service, but when you have twenty services, you need twenty rate limiter configurations. With APIM, one rate-limiting policy applies to all APIs managed by the gateway. The same applies to authentication — validate the JWT once at the gateway, and your services receive a trusted request with the user identity in a header.

sections.title: The Policy Pipeline — Four Phases That Replace Dozens of Java Filters
sections.content:
The policy pipeline is APIM's core mechanism. Each API operation has policies that execute in four phases, and each phase can modify the request, response, or trigger error handling.

```xml
<policies>
  <inbound>
    <validate-jwt header-name="Authorization"
                  failed-validation-httpcode="401">
      <openid-config url="https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/
        v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration" />
      <required-claims>
        <claim name="aud"><value>api://my-api</value></claim>
      </required-claims>
    </validate-jwt>
    <rate-limit-by-key calls="100" renewal-period="60"
      counter-key="@(context.Subscription.Id)" />
    <cache-lookup vary-by-developer="true" />
  </inbound>
  <backend>
    <forward-request />
  </backend>
  <outbound>
    <cache-store duration="300" />
    <set-header name="X-Powered-By" exists-action="delete" />
  </outbound>
  <on-error>
    <return-response>
      <set-status code="500" reason="Internal Error" />
    </return-response>
  </on-error>
</policies>
```

Policies support **C#-like expressions** for dynamic values — `@(context.Subscription.Id)` accesses the caller's subscription key, `@(context.Request.Headers.GetValueOrDefault("X-Custom", ""))` reads headers. This expressiveness lets you implement complex routing logic — A/B testing by percentage, tenant-specific rate limits, conditional header injection — without deploying custom code.

The inbound `cache-lookup` and outbound `cache-store` work together to cache GET responses at the gateway level. For read-heavy catalog APIs, this reduces backend load by 60–80% without any caching code in your Spring Boot service.

sections.title: OpenAPI Import Keeps APIM in Sync With Your Spring Controllers
sections.content:
APIM includes a **hosted developer portal** where API consumers browse documentation, test endpoints interactively, and manage their subscription keys. This replaces the need to build and maintain separate API documentation infrastructure.

The integration point with Spring Boot is OpenAPI. Add `springdoc-openapi` to your service to generate an OpenAPI spec, then import it into APIM. APIM creates API operations, request/response schemas, and validation rules directly from the spec.

```bash
az apim api import \
  --resource-group my-rg \
  --service-name my-apim \
  --api-id order-api \
  --path /orders \
  --specification-format OpenApiJson \
  --specification-url https://order-api.internal/v3/api-docs
```

This keeps APIM definitions synchronized with your code. When you add a new endpoint to your Spring controller, regenerate and re-import the OpenAPI spec — APIM picks up the new operation without manual portal configuration.

For API versioning, APIM supports three schemes: URL path (`/v1/orders`), query parameter (`?api-version=2024-01`), and HTTP header. URL path versioning is the most widely adopted because it's visible in URLs and easy for consumers to understand. APIM's **version sets** group versions together, and **revisions** handle backward-compatible changes within a version — deploy a revision, test it, then make it the current version. This separation between breaking changes (versions) and non-breaking changes (revisions) prevents the version proliferation that plagues many API platforms.

sections.title: Self-Hosted Gateway Runs Policies Locally When Data Can't Leave Your Network
sections.content:
For organizations with data residency requirements or hybrid cloud deployments, APIM's **self-hosted gateway** runs as a container in your own infrastructure — on-premises data centers, edge locations, or other cloud providers. Policies are managed centrally in Azure, but the gateway executes them locally.

This addresses a common compliance concern: regulated industries (healthcare, finance) may require that API traffic not traverse the public internet. The self-hosted gateway processes requests within your network boundary while reporting telemetry and receiving policy updates from the Azure control plane.

The gateway container runs as a Kubernetes deployment or Docker container, and it downloads policies from APIM on startup and periodically afterward. If connectivity to Azure is temporarily lost, the gateway continues operating with cached policies — it doesn't go down when the control plane is unreachable. This makes it practical for edge deployments with intermittent connectivity.

The trade-off is operational responsibility: you manage the container's lifecycle, scaling, and networking. For organizations that already run Kubernetes, adding the gateway container to the cluster is straightforward. For those that don't, the managed APIM gateway in Azure is the simpler choice.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **JWT validation at the gateway eliminates per-service auth code** — `validate-jwt` policy validates Azure AD tokens; unauthorized requests rejected before reaching the backend; reduces attack surface
- **Rate limiting per subscription key without backend code** — `rate-limit-by-key` policy; per-client throttling; configurable window and call count; overflow returns 429 with Retry-After header automatically
- **Request/response transformation in XML policies** — add correlation IDs to inbound headers; strip internal headers from outbound responses; transform JSON structure between gateway and backend versions
- **Gateway caching for read-heavy APIs** — `cache-lookup` and `cache-store` policies; cache GET responses at the gateway; configurable TTL; Spring Boot service receives only cache-miss requests
- **Auto-generated developer portal from OpenAPI** — import `/v3/api-docs` from Spring Boot; portal provides interactive API documentation and testing; eliminates manual Swagger maintenance

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Azure API Management (APIM) sits in front of Spring Boot microservices as an API gateway, handling cross-cutting concerns — authentication, rate limiting, request transformation, caching, and API documentation — without putting that logic in each service.

**What APIM handles**
- Authentication: validate JWT tokens from Azure AD at the gateway before requests reach the backend — which means unauthorized requests are rejected at the edge without consuming backend resources
- Rate limiting: apply throttling policies per subscription key, per IP, or per user — `rate-limit-by-key` with a configurable window and call limit prevents one client from consuming all capacity
- Request/response transformation: add or strip headers, transform JSON, route requests based on content — `set-header` and `set-body` policies modify requests without changing backend code
- Caching: `cache-lookup` and `cache-store` policies cache GET responses at the gateway — which means repeated identical requests return cached responses without hitting the Spring Boot service

**Policy expressions**
- APIM policies are XML-based and run in four processing phases: inbound (before the backend), backend (controls the backend call), outbound (transforms the response), and on-error (handles exceptions)
- `<rate-limit-by-key calls="100" renewal-period="60" counter-key="@(context.Subscription.Id)" />` limits each subscription to 100 calls per minute without any rate limiting code in the Spring Boot service

**Backend service registration**
- Register Spring Boot services as APIM backends with their internal URL — ECS tasks behind an internal ALB, AKS services behind an internal load balancer, or App Service custom domains
- APIM calls the backend URL with backend policies applied; the Spring Boot service doesn't know APIM exists; it just receives HTTP requests as normal

**Developer portal**
- APIM auto-generates an API documentation portal from OpenAPI/Swagger definitions — import the Spring Boot service's `/v3/api-docs` endpoint; developers explore and test APIs from the portal
